claim: The Swiss HIV Cohort Study (SHCS) is a multicenter, nationwide, prospective observational study of HIV infected individuals in Switzerland, established in 1988.
source: The SHCS is a multicenter, nationwide, prospective observational study of HIV infected individuals in Switzerland, established in 1988 (Swiss HIV Cohort Study et al., 2010).
evidence: Supported by citation to Swiss HIV Cohort Study et al., 2010

claim: Up to December 2016 over 19,500 patients have been enrolled in the SHCS.
source: Up to December 2016 over 19,500 patients have been enrolled.
evidence: Direct statement of enrollment numbers

claim: The SHCS covers more than 75% HIV-positive individuals on antiretroviral therapy (ART) in Switzerland.
source: The SHCS is highly-representative as it covers more than 75% HIV-positive individuals on antiretroviral therapy (ART) in Switzerland (Swiss HIV Cohort Study et al., 2010).
evidence: Supported by citation to Swiss HIV Cohort Study et al., 2010

claim: For approximately 60% of the SHCS patients at least one partial pol sequence from the genotypic resistance testing is available.
source: In addition to the extensive demographic and clinical data collected at biannual/quarterly follow-up (FUP) visits, for approximately 60% of the patients at least one partial pol sequence from the genotypic resistance testing is available (in total 22,036 sequences from the SHCS resistance database until August 2015).
evidence: Direct statement of sequence availability with specific numbers

claim: The patients with heterosexual contact as the most likely transmission route comprise about one third of all SHCS participants.
source: The patients with heterosexual contact as the most likely transmission route comprise about one third of all SHCS participants.
evidence: Direct statement of proportion

claim: 3,100 transmission clusters among heterosexuals in the SHCS were identified.
source: We identified 3,100 transmission clusters among heterosexuals in the SHCS.
evidence: Direct statement of identified clusters

claim: The transmission clusters among heterosexuals in the SHCS were small in size.
source: These clusters were small in size (Table 1)
evidence: Supported by reference to Table 1 showing cluster size distribution

claim: 1,133 transmission chains were classified as being of Swiss origin.
source: Based on the most likely geographic origin of the transmission clusters, we classified 1,133 transmission chains as being of Swiss origin, that is, to represent introductions from other transmission groups in Switzerland into the heterosexual population
evidence: Direct statement of classification results

claim: 1,967 transmission chains were classified as being of non-Swiss origin.
source: and 1,967 to be of non-Swiss origin.
evidence: Direct statement of classification results

claim: For transmission chains of non-Swiss origin, the R0 of the index case was reduced by a factor of ρindex=0.35.
source: For these latter transmission chains, we assumed that the R0 of the index case was reduced by a factor of ρindex=0.35 (see Materials and methods).
evidence: Direct statement of model assumption

claim: The subtype-depending sampling probabilities were fixed based on the results from the study by Shilaih et al. (2016), corrected by the proportion of the HIV infected individuals linked to care (80% based on Kohler et al., 2015) and the fraction of heterosexuals from the SHCS with an HIV sequence in the phylogenetic tree (57.22%).
source: To take into account the imperfect sampling density we fixed the subtype-depending sampling probabilities based on the results from the study by Shilaih et al. (2016), corrected by the proportion of the HIV infected individuals linked to care (80% based on Kohler et al., 2015) and the fraction of heterosexuals from the SHCS with an HIV sequence in the phylogenetic tree (57.22%).
evidence: Supported by citations to Shilaih et al., 2016 and Kohler et al., 2015, with specific percentages provided

claim: The overall R0 for HIV transmission in Swiss heterosexuals is estimated to be 0.44 (95%-confidence interval 0.42—0.46).
source: In this baseline model the R0 was estimated to be 0.44 (95%-confidence interval (CI) 0.42—0.46).
evidence: Direct statement of statistical estimate with confidence interval

claim: The R0 for HIV transmission in Swiss heterosexuals is clearly below 1.
source: The fact that R0 was clearly below 1 (p-value <0.001 from one-sided Wald hypothesis testing H0:R0=1 against the alternative HA:R0<1) indicated that HIV transmission is far away from a self-sustained epidemic.
evidence: Supported by statistical testing with p-value

claim: HIV transmission among Swiss heterosexuals is far away from a self-sustained epidemic.
source: The fact that R0 was clearly below 1 (p-value <0.001 from one-sided Wald hypothesis testing H0:R0=1 against the alternative HA:R0<1) indicated that HIV transmission is far away from a self-sustained epidemic.
evidence: Inference based on R0 being significantly below 1

claim: Subtype B has an estimated R0 of 0.35 (95%-CI 0.33—0.39).
source: The subtype-stratified analyses indeed yielded lower R0 of 0.35 (95%-CI 0.33—0.39) for subtype B as compared to the non-B subtypes (Figure 1).
evidence: Direct statement of statistical estimate with reference to Figure 1

claim: CRF02_AG has the highest estimated R0 of 0.62 (95%-CI 0.56—0.69) among all subtypes.
source: The recombinant form CRF02_AG had the highest estimated R0 of 0.62 (95%-CI 0.56—0.69).
evidence: Direct statement of statistical estimate

claim: All HIV subtypes have R0 estimates significantly below 1.
source: Despite these differences among the R0 estimates for different subtypes they were all significantly below 1 (with all p-values from the one-sided test smaller than 0.001).
evidence: Supported by statistical testing with p-values

claim: There is no danger of a self-sustained HIV epidemic in Swiss heterosexuals of any HIV subtype.
source: Therefore, we concluded that there is no danger of a self-sustained HIV epidemic in Swiss heterosexuals of any HIV subtype.
evidence: Conclusion based on all subtypes having R0 significantly below 1

claim: The overall R0 is decreasing at a factor 0.89 per 10 years (95%-CI 0.83—0.96).
source: We found that overall the R0 is decreasing at a factor 0.89 per 10 years (95%-CI 0.83—0.96).
evidence: Direct statement of statistical estimate from univariate model

claim: The per subtype-stratified analyses showed consistently decreasing time trend among the subtypes ranging from factor 0.65 per 10 years for subtype A to 0.89 for B-subtype.
source: The per subtype-stratified analyses showed the consistently decreasing time trend among the subtypes ranging from factor 0.65 per 10 years for subtype A to 0.89 for B-subtype.
evidence: Direct statement of stratified analysis results

claim: A cubic spline (without the linear term) was identified as the optimal model for R0 time trend according to the Bayesian information criterion (BIC).
source: With the reference date on the 1st of January 1996 (which corresponds to the median estimated date of infection - see Table 2) a cubic spline (without the linear term) was identified as the optimal model according to the Bayesian information criterion (BIC).
evidence: Direct statement of model selection result

claim: The cubic spline model exhibits a mild increase of the R0 from the mid 1980's to the mid 1990's.
source: This model exhibits a mild increase of the R0 from the mid 1980's to the mid 1990's
evidence: Direct statement of model results

claim: The peak-R0 of 0.49 (95%-CI 0.46—0.53) was reached in 1996.
source: with a peak-R0 of 0.49 (95%-CI 0.46—0.53) reached in 1996
evidence: Direct statement of statistical estimate

claim: The time of peak-R0 coincided with the introduction of highly active antiretroviral therapy.
source: It is noteworthy that the time of peak-R0 coincided with the introduction of highly active antiretroviral therapy.
evidence: Temporal association noted between peak R0 and HAART introduction

claim: Shortly after the peak-R0 in 1996, the R0 started to rapidly decrease and has never rebounded.
source: Shortly after the R0 started to rapidly decrease and has never rebounded.
evidence: Direct statement of trend observation

claim: All non-B subtypes have higher R0 compared to subtype B.
source: The simplest model containing only the linear terms of risk factors showed that the R0 is decreasing with the establishment date of the transmission chain and that all non-B subtypes have higher R0 compared to subtype B
evidence: Direct statement of multivariate model results

claim: Reporting sex with occasional partners is associated with higher R0.
source: Moreover, we found that reporting sex with occasional partners and longer time to HIV diagnosis of the index case are associated with higher R0
evidence: Direct statement of multivariate model results

claim: Longer time to HIV diagnosis of the index case is associated with higher R0.
source: Moreover, we found that reporting sex with occasional partners and longer time to HIV diagnosis of the index case are associated with higher R0
evidence: Direct statement of multivariate model results

claim: The earliest CD4 cell count does not have significant effects on R0.
source: whereas the earliest CD4 cell count and the age do not have significant effects (Figure 3).
evidence: Direct statement of multivariate model results with reference to Figure 3

claim: Age does not have significant effects on R0.
source: whereas the earliest CD4 cell count and the age do not have significant effects (Figure 3).
evidence: Direct statement of multivariate model results with reference to Figure 3

claim: The final multivariate model identified subtype, establishment date of the transmission chain, frequency of reporting sex with occasional partner and time to diagnosis of the index case as the significant risk factors associated with R0.
source: The final multivariate model identified subtype, establishment date of the transmission chain, frequency of reporting sex with occasional partner and time to diagnosis of the index case as the significant risk factors associated with R0 (see Selection of the predictive models).
evidence: Direct statement of final model results

claim: There is a steep increase of R0 in the early/acute phase of the infection.
source: The steep increase of R0 in the early/acute phase (see Figure 4) of the infection indicates the importance of early diagnosis
evidence: Observation from Figure 4 showing nonlinear relationship

claim: The steep increase of R0 in the early/acute phase of infection indicates the importance of early diagnosis.
source: The steep increase of R0 in the early/acute phase (see Figure 4) of the infection indicates the importance of early diagnosis (which is nowadays closely related to early treatment initiation) while the time becomes less relevant in the cases diagnosed late in the chronic phase.
evidence: Inference drawn from the observed relationship in Figure 4

claim: Viral sequences combined with basic demographic information can be successfully used to estimate the basic reproductive number R0 of HIV in a subcritical setting.
source: Our approach demonstrates that viral sequences combined with basic demographic information can be successfully used not only to estimate the basic reproductive number R0 of HIV in a subcritical setting and thereby assess the danger of a generalized HIV epidemic but also to shed light on the trends and other determinants of viral transmission.
evidence: Conclusion based on the demonstrated methodology and results

claim: The approach can be used to assess the danger of a generalized HIV epidemic.
source: Our approach demonstrates that viral sequences combined with basic demographic information can be successfully used not only to estimate the basic reproductive number R0 of HIV in a subcritical setting and thereby assess the danger of a generalized HIV epidemic but also to shed light on the trends and other determinants of viral transmission.
evidence: Conclusion based on the demonstrated methodology and results

claim: The approach can shed light on the trends and other determinants of viral transmission.
source: Our approach demonstrates that viral sequences combined with basic demographic information can be successfully used not only to estimate the basic reproductive number R0 of HIV in a subcritical setting and thereby assess the danger of a generalized HIV epidemic but also to shed light on the trends and other determinants of viral transmission.
evidence: Conclusion based on the demonstrated methodology and results

claim: The HIV epidemic in Switzerland is and most likely will remain restricted to high risk core groups, especially MSM.
source: Hence, the HIV epidemic in Switzerland is and most likely will remain restricted to high risk core groups, especially MSM.
evidence: Conclusion based on R0 estimates being below 1 and decreasing

claim: The results suggest that integrated prevention measures in Switzerland taken over time were successful within the heterosexual population.
source: Moreover, the results suggest that integrated prevention measures in Switzerland taken over time were successful within the heterosexual population.
evidence: Inference drawn from decreasing R0 trend

claim: In most resource-rich settings HIV transmission is concentrated, driven mostly by transmission among men who have sex with men (MSM) and injecting drug users (IDU).
source: In most resource-rich settings HIV transmission is concentrated, that is, driven mostly by transmission among men who have sex with men (MSM) and injecting drug users (IDU), whereas the limited transmission among heterosexuals is maintained by either imported infections or spillovers from other transmission groups (Kouyos et al., 2010; von Wyl et al., 2011; Ragonnet-Cronin et al., 2016; Xiridou et al., 2010; Esbjörnsson et al., 2016; Sallam et al., 2017).
evidence: Supported by multiple citations

claim: Limited transmission among heterosexuals in resource-rich settings is maintained by either imported infections or spillovers from other transmission groups.
source: In most resource-rich settings HIV transmission is concentrated, that is, driven mostly by transmission among men who have sex with men (MSM) and injecting drug users (IDU), whereas the limited transmission among heterosexuals is maintained by either imported infections or spillovers from other transmission groups (Kouyos et al., 2010; von Wyl et al., 2011; Ragonnet-Cronin et al., 2016; Xiridou et al., 2010; Esbjörnsson et al., 2016; Sallam et al., 2017).
evidence: Supported by multiple citations

claim: In most Western European countries and similar epidemiological settings the basic reproductive number R0 among heterosexuals is below 1.
source: This suggests that in most Western European countries and similar epidemiological settings the basic reproductive number R0 among heterosexuals is below 1.
evidence: Inference based on concentrated epidemic pattern

claim: The distribution of outbreak sizes can be used to quantify pathogen spread for stage III zoonoses and tuberculosis.
source: For the case of stage III zoonoses and tuberculosis, it has been shown that the distribution of outbreak sizes can be used to quantify the pathogen spread (Blumberg and Lloyd-Smith, 2013b; Blumberg and Lloyd-Smith, 2013a; Borgdorff et al., 1998).
evidence: Supported by citations to Blumberg and Lloyd-Smith, 2013b; Blumberg and Lloyd-Smith, 2013a; Borgdorff et al., 1998

claim: HIV has long infectious periods in the absence of treatment.
source: Compared to the animal-human transmission the delayed introduction of the index case of an STI or blood-borne virus to the subpopulation of interest plays an important role, especially in viruses like HIV with long infectious periods in the absence of treatment and higher transmissibility during the acute phase (Marzel et al., 2016; Powers et al., 2011; Rieder et al., 2010; Rodger et al., 2016; Hollingsworth et al., 2008; Cohen et al., 2011b; Cohen et al., 2011a; Cohen et al., 2016).
evidence: Supported by multiple citations

claim: HIV has higher transmissibility during the acute phase.
source: Compared to the animal-human transmission the delayed introduction of the index case of an STI or blood-borne virus to the subpopulation of interest plays an important role, especially in viruses like HIV with long infectious periods in the absence of treatment and higher transmissibility during the acute phase (Marzel et al., 2016; Powers et al., 2011; Rieder et al., 2010; Rodger et al., 2016; Hollingsworth et al., 2008; Cohen et al., 2011b; Cohen et al., 2011a; Cohen et al., 2016).
evidence: Supported by multiple citations

claim: A considerable fraction of HIV cases in heterosexuals is found in migrants.
source: This is especially important because a considerable fraction of HIV cases in heterosexuals is found in migrants (Del Amo et al., 2004; von Wyl et al., 2011; European Centre for Disease Prevention and Control/WHO Regional Office for Europe, 2016).
evidence: Supported by citations to Del Amo et al., 2004; von Wyl et al., 2011; European Centre for Disease Prevention and Control/WHO Regional Office for Europe, 2016

claim: The phylogenetic tree was constructed from 10,840 SHCS and 90,933 background sequences.
source: Using the earliest available of the remaining sequences for each patient, the phylogenetic tree was built with the FastTree algorithm under the generalized time-reversible model of nucleotide evolution (Price et al., 2009) including 10,840 SHCS and 90,933 background sequences.
evidence: Direct statement of data used in phylogenetic tree construction

claim: The phylogenetic tree was built with the FastTree algorithm under the generalized time-reversible model of nucleotide evolution.
source: Using the earliest available of the remaining sequences for each patient, the phylogenetic tree was built with the FastTree algorithm under the generalized time-reversible model of nucleotide evolution (Price et al., 2009) including 10,840 SHCS and 90,933 background sequences.
evidence: Direct statement of methodology with citation

claim: The Swiss heterosexual transmission chains were defined as clusters in the phylogenetic tree containing exclusively Swiss HIV sequences from individuals with heterosexual contact as the most likely route of the transmission.
source: The Swiss heterosexual transmission chains were defined as clusters in the phylogenetic tree containing exclusively Swiss HIV sequences from individuals with heterosexual contact as the most likely route of the transmission, regardless of the respective genetic distances and local support values
evidence: Direct statement of operational definition

claim: Omitting the reduced transmissibility of the index case leads to largely underestimated R0 (overall R0 of 0.33, 95%-CI 0.31—0.35).
source: On the one hand, omitting the reduced transmissibility of the index case, that is, assuming ρindex=1, leads to largely underestimated R0 (overall R0 of 0.33, 95%-CI 0.31—0.35) affirming the importance of this extension.
evidence: Results from sensitivity analysis

claim: When lowering the ρindex for transmission chains of non-Swiss origin to 0.25, the R0 estimate is 0.47 (95%-CI 0.44—0.49).
source: To address this issue we lowered the ρindex for the transmission chains of non-Swiss origin to 0.25 to obtain a more conservative estimate of R0, which was, nevertheless, still safely below 1 (0.47, 95%-CI 0.44—0.49).
evidence: Results from sensitivity analysis

claim: The mean time to being non-infectious is approximately 2—2.5 years in recent years.
source: However, given much higher transmissibility of HIV in the acute and recent infection (Marzel et al., 2016) and estimated mean time to being non-infectious of approximately 2—2.5 years in recent years (Stadler et al., 2012; Hughes et al., 2009)
evidence: Supported by citations to Stadler et al., 2012; Hughes et al., 2009

claim: Epidemiological differences between the HIV-1 subtypes, especially between B and non-B subtypes, have been pointed out previously.
source: Epidemiological differences between the HIV-1 subtypes, especially between B and non-B subtypes, have been pointed out previously (Kouyos et al., 2010; von Wyl et al., 2011).
evidence: Supported by citations to Kouyos et al., 2010; von Wyl et al., 2011

source: For instance, the CRF01_AE is often found in Asians and it also most likely originates from Southeastern Asia (Angelis et al., 2015)

claim: The approach can be easily used in other non-self-sustained epidemics since viral sequences from genotypic resistance testing are nowadays routinely produced in most resource-rich settings.
source: Even though the Swiss HIV epidemic is captured in outstanding detail and representativeness by the SHCS, our approach can be easily used in other non-self-sustained epidemics since viral sequences from genotypic resistance testing are nowadays routinely produced in most resource-rich settings.
